newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Searching for buyers.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Searching for buyers.

text.p: Asian crude sellers are searching for buyers this week amid a dearth of bullish news to spark fresh demand.
West African imports, a raft of turnarounds at refineries and impending gas oil imports into Asia are allowing buyers to adopt a relaxed buying strategy, traders said.
"If you can get cheaper barrels later, then you just wait," one trader said. "The market looks weak, and people expect that to roll forward."

Middle East grades, trading for May lifting, have been mostly trading flat to their official selling prices, with some exceptions, including an Umm Shaif cargo sold last week at a premium of ADNOC +14 cents, about 12 cents higher than the previous deal.
Traders said field maintenance in May by ADNOC is having only a limited affect on the market because it has built up sufficient inventories to meet buyers' needs.
A narrowing Brent/Dubai has prompted as many as seven April loading very large crude carriers (VLCC) of West African grades. Most spot deals have been done into South Korea and China.
Traders said the imports might slow with a rise in freight rates, but the imports have been high enough to prompt perception of an amply supplied Asian market, traders said.
NYMEX crudes temporarily slipping to contango in the near market last week and Brent doing the same in London on Friday have further undermined market sentiment, traders said.
May Brent settled on Friday at $19.99 per barrel, at a two-cents contango. The last time the front-month and the second position were in contango was for four days in July 1995.
"These things feed on themselves. Once people believe they can buy cheap on a prompt basis the contango lasts longer," a trader said.
The weak market is also being fuelled by worries of gas oil imports, which would hit refinery margins.
The imports, estimated to be at least 800,000 tonnes, are expected from Russia, the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and could start arriving from mid April.
However, a lot of the volume is expected to be absorbed by India.
The key for regional grades, trading for lifting during April, remains China, traders said.
Traders said the energy giant has little appetite to buy first-half April cargoes and recent purchases of Cabinda from West Africa would reduce its need for Minas crude.
Minas and Duri, which has an overhang from March into April, both traded last week at ICP less 15/25 cents.
Producers are holding out for ICP flat.

But traders said the return to production of the 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) Dumai refinery, after scheduled maintenance and the 125,000 bpd Balongan refinery, after an unexpected shut down, would help to support the Minas and Duri markets.
